The session opened on one question for the room, “How are you using AI today?” Attendees traded what they already use it for and their time-saving shortcuts.
A model is like a student made to read most of the internet: it learns patterns without understanding them and predicts one word at a time. That is why it can miss nuance or invent facts.

Most work needs one generalist, such as ChatGPT, Gemini or Copilot. Know when to call a specialist: Perplexity when an answer needs citations, Claude for very long reports, Copilot inside Word, Excel and Outlook, NotebookLM for your own files.

A prompt works like a brief to a very literal assistant. H4W covers who you are, what you need, why, who it is for and how it should look; COSTAR adds context, objective, style, tone, audience and response.
Then where AI fits in a working day: a long report turned into a few key points, a hard email started from a first draft instead of a blank page, and messy meeting notes turned into action items.

How the pieces differ: a skill holds the know-how for a task, an MCP server connects the model to outside tools and data, and a plugin packages these to install in one step.
A workflow runs the same steps every time; an agent works toward a goal and chooses its own steps, including which workflow to call.

Retrieval-augmented generation lets the model look things up in an organization’s documents first. It finds the passages that matter, adds them to the prompt and answers from them, so its answers rest on that organization’s information.

A Project is the room where files and instructions wait; a skill is a recipe you carry into any room. In a Project, Claude explained a repair center’s overtime from the notes; a chat with no files guessed.

Grounding works like an open-book exam: the model finds the passages that match, sets them beside the request, and answers from them. Hand it an outdated file and you get a confident, outdated answer.

Plan Big, Run Small, Check with the Graph
A node is a noun, an edge is a verb and a property is an adjective. Models draft the graph, people verify it, and only verified edges are the authority.
The same shape relabels in place, from a patient, her doctor and her drugs to a client, its payment service, the server it runs on, a change and an incident.
Before the model, the graph finds the facts that matter and a verified example of a good answer. Asked if a patient with a penicillin allergy can take amoxicillin, the model gave a safe no.
For a failing payment service, the same path led through its server to a library upgrade seventeen minutes before the incident, and to a rollback.
After the model, an agent’s answer becomes a chain of claims tested against the graph. Blaming the data centre failed and went back as feedback; naming the change passed.
The graph is only an authority while someone keeps it current.
Small models fit in the room

A small model runs on one laptop or one GPU, usually under fifteen billion parameters. It keeps data in the building, but reasons less well and needs sharper prompts, evaluation and often fine-tuning.

Four sliders set the choice: how sensitive the data is, how many requests, how hard the thinking and how fast the answer. Hard thinking on secret data meant the largest open model your hardware allows.
Then the setup, in three commands: install Ollama, run Gemma 4 12B, and call the same model as an API on the laptop.

A small model does not want a conversation; it wants a task. A vague question about a payment problem got a generic answer. A narrow task with the graph’s facts named the change and the rollback.

A Multi-Layer Framework for Evaluating the Return on Investment of AI Projects
Enterprise AI spending is projected to exceed $1.8 trillion by 2030, yet more than 80 percent of AI projects fail to deliver measurable returns.

Traditional capital budgeting tools were designed for investments with well-defined cash flows and fail to account for the unique risk characteristics of AI: deeply uncertain cost structures, indirect and non-linear benefits, path-dependent value creation, and acute sensitivity to organizational readiness.

This paper proposes a multi-layer framework that integrates four complementary analytical lenses into a coherent AI investment decision process: a SCALE strategic readiness assessment (Layer 0), ROIC decomposition through a value driver tree (Layer 1), stage-gate phased investment (Layer 2), and a synthesized decision scorecard (Layer 3).

We complement these layers with a novel eight-category risk-adjustment table that systematically adjusts the discount rate to reflect AI-specific risks, including vendor and platform dependency and organizational friction, two dimensions that existing frameworks ignore.

We validate the framework against eight real-world AI deployments spanning four deployment categories: B2B (Salesforce Agentforce, validated against Palantir), B2C (Spotify, validated against Duolingo), Platform (Shopify Magic, validated against Uber), and Internal (JPMorgan COiN, validated against NatWest).

The framework's contribution is not a new financial formula; it is a structured methodology that forces decision-makers to systematically confront the full range of factors determining AI project outcomes, in an environment where the dominant failure mode is not bad technology but unexamined assumptions.
Who Trains the Next Senior? Managing Software Engineering When AI Makes Code Cheap
Generative and agentic AI have made the routine work of software engineering nearly free, and the first casualty is the junior engineer.
Engineering leaders now face a choice most are making by default.

Cheap machine-made code commoditizes breadth, the plausible and conventional, while raising the value of two things humans still supply and machines do not: depth, the judgment of which answer is right in this system, and divergence, the perspective from outside the consensus that a senior-plus-AI team structurally lacks.
Left to inertia, organizations slide into substitution, replacing juniors and letting review, apprenticeship, and the diversity of what they build hollow out.

The alternative, complementarity, is a set of concrete moves: shrink the unit of review, tier scrutiny by consequence, measure verified outcomes rather than raw output, and rebuild the apprenticeship on purpose.
We show why the choice is real, what each path costs, and what to do about it now.
Drone-Megaddon: A Real-Time Strategy Interface for Managing Drone Swarms
Neural sensors, Oculus Rift, mobile devices - to date, drone researchers have utilized a variety of diﬀerent media to control a single drone.
However, to the best of our knowledge, there are currently no adequate solutions for dealing with multiple drones at a time.
So, in this paper, we describe Drone-Megaddon, an Android-based real-time strategy interface patterned after the hit RTS game StarCraft II, which facilitates high-level management of a drone swarm.
Drone-Megaddon 2026: Co-Intelligent Swarm Control with Language and Vision Models
In 2014, we introduced Drone-Megaddon, an Android interface for managing drone swarms, patterned after real time strategy (RTS) video games like StarCraft II.
We argued that its select-then-execute paradigm fit commanding multiple drones better than the single drone piloting interfaces available at the time.
Twelve years later, three things around it have changed.
Commercial drones now ship with LTE connectivity and with navigation modes built for environments where GPS is denied.
Drone warfare at scale has generated a public body of operational lessons on electronic warfare and operator load.
And foundation models have made natural language intent and visual grounding tractable as interfaces to robotic systems.
The third change is the one this paper turns on.
We propose a successor to Drone-Megaddon that keeps the 2014 core: RTS selection, the $RAD command queue, ACK’d radio, and human oversight.
Over that core we propose three AI layers.
The intent translator takes an operator utterance together with the currently selected drones and the map state, and emits a validated sequence of $RAD commands.
The perception grounder takes a referring expression such as “follow the red sedan” together with the drone’s current video feed, and emits a tracked bounding box bound to a specific drone.

The coordination planner takes a single waypoint intended for multiple drones and emits one distinct final position per drone, addressing what the 2014 paper called the random offset at destination behavior.
We describe each layer at the level of its interface, walk through a search-and-rescue example, and address ethical considerations the 2014 paper did not engage with.
